L8@P0: Abstract. Symbolic Model Checking [3, 14] has proven to be a powerful technique for the verification of reactive systems. BDDs [2] have traditionally been
L9@P0: used as a symbolic representation of the system. In this paper we show how
L10@P0: boolean decision procedures, like St˚almarck’s Method [16] or the Davis & Putnam Procedure [7], can replace BDDs. This new technique avoids the space blow
L11@P0: up of BDDs, generates counterexamples much faster, and sometimes speeds up
L12@P0: the verification. In addition, it produces counterexamples of minimal length. We
L13@P0: introduce a bounded model checking procedure for LTL which reduces model
L14@P0: checking to propositional satisfiability. We show that bounded LTL model checking can be done without a tableau construction. We have implemented a model
L15@P0: checker BMC, based on bounded model checking, and preliminary results are
L16@P0: presented.

L42@P1: generate a propositional formula that is satisfiable iff such a counterexample exists. In
L43@P1: particular, we introduce the notion of bounded model checking, where the bound is the

L180@P4: The basic idea of bounded model checking is to consider only a finite prefix of a path
L181@P4: that may be a solution to an existential model checking problem. We restrict the length
L182@P4: of the prefix by a certain bound k. In practice we progressively increase the bound,
L183@P4: looking for longer and longer possible counterexamples.
L184@P4: A crucial observation is that, though the prefix of a path is finite, it still might represent an infinite path if there is a back loop from the last state of the prefix to any of the
L185@P4: previous states (see Figure 2(b)). If there is no such back loop (see Figure 2(a)), then
L186@P4: the prefix does not say anything about the infinite behavior of the path. For instance,
L187@P4: only a prefix with a back loop can represent a witness for Gp. Even if p holds along all
L188@P4: the states from s0 to sk, but there is no back loop from sk to a previous state, then we
L189@P4: cannot conclude that we have found a witness for Gp, since p might not hold at sk+1.

L514@P9: semantics if we consider all possible bounds. This equivalence leads to a straightforward LTL model checking procedure. To check whether M j= Ef , the procedure checks
L515@P9: M j=k Ef for k = 0; 1; 2;:::. If M j=k Ef , then the procedure proves that M j= Ef and
L516@P9: produces a witness of length k. If M 6j= Ef , we have to increment the value of k indefinitely, and the procedure does not terminate. In this section we establish several bounds
L517@P9: on k. If M 6j=k Ef for all k within the bound, we conclude that M 6j= Ef .
L518@P9: 5.1 ECTL
L519@P9: ECTL is a subset of ECTL* where each temporal operator is preceded by one existential
L520@P9: path quantifier. We have extended bounded model checking to handle ECTL formulas.
L521@P9: Semantics and translation for ECTL formulas can be found in the full version of this
L522@P9: paper. In general, better bounds can be derived for ECTL formulas than for LTL formulas. The intersection of the two sets of formulas includes many temporal properties of
L523@P9: practical interest (e.g. EFp and EGp). Therefore, we include the discussion of bounds
L524@P9: for ECTL formulas in this section.

L526@P9: number of states in M, then M j= Ef iff there exists k jMj with M j=k Ef.
L527@P9: In symbolic model checking, the number of states in a Kripke structure is bounded
L528@P9: by 2n, where n is the number of boolean variables to encode the Kripke structure.
L529@P9: Typical model checking problems involve Kripke structures with tens or hundreds of
L530@P9: boolean variables. The bound given in Theorem 18 is often too large for practical problems.

L571@P10: 5.2 LTL
